That is the careful version,\n17\twritten by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a\n18\tconfidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.\n19\t\n20\tThe registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer\n21\tto implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —\n41\tit does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and\n42\tthere is no opt-out flag.\n43\t\n44\tUpdate `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.\n45\t\n46\t## Acceptance criteria\n47\t\n48\t- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's\n49\t      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; A chain like `a.b.c.d` or `a.b().c.d()`\n * reaches through collaborators the caller has no business knowing; the\n * caller should ask its direct collaborator for what it needs.\n *\n * Depth = number of `MemberExpression` hops from the chain's root. Computed\n * hops (`a[0].b`) and optional hops (`a?.b`) count like any other. Only the\n * OUTERMOST member expression of a chain is reported — an inner one whose\n * parent continues the chain (as the object of another member, or as the\n * callee of a call that is itself continued) is skipped.\n *\n * Exempt:\n *  - the root is `this` / `super`;\n *  - the root is a well-known global (`Math`, `JSON`, `Promise`, `Object`,\n *    `Array`, `Number`, `String`, `Reflect`, `process`, `console`,\n *    `globalThis`, `window`, `document`, `Symbol`, `Date`) or a name listed\n *    in option `allowRoots`;\n *  - every hop after the root is a call (`builder().a().b().c()` fluent\n *    chains return the same kind of thing at each step);\n *  - chains rooted in `import.meta`.\n *\n * Detect-only: the fix is a method on the direct collaborator.\n */\nconst DEFAULT_MAX = 2;\nconst CHAIN_TEXT_LIMIT = 60;\nconst DEFAULT_ALLOWED_ROOTS = new Set([\n    \"Math\",\n    \"JSON\",\n    \"Promise\",\n    \"Object\",\n    \"Array\",\n    \"Number\",\n    \"String\",\n    \"Reflect\",\n    \"process\",\n    \"console\",\n    \"globalThis\",\n    \"window\",\n    \"document\",\n    \"Symbol\",\n    \"Date\",\n]);\nconst EXEMPT_ROOT_TYPES = new Set([\"ThisExpression\", \"Super\", \"MetaProperty\"]);\nconst TRANSPARENT_WRAPPERS = new Set([\n    \"ChainExpression\",\n    \"TSNonNullExpression\",\n]);\nfunction isCalled(node) {\n    const parent = node.parent;\n    return (Boolean(parent) &&\n        parent.type === \"CallExpression\" &&\n        parent.callee === node);\n}\nfunction continuesChain(node) {\n    const parent = node.parent;\n    if (!parent) {\n        return false;\n    }\n    if (parent.type === \"MemberExpression\") {\n        return parent.object === node;\n    }\n    const isTransparentWrapper = isCalled(node) || TRANSPARENT_WRAPPERS.has(parent.type);\n    return isTransparentWrapper && continuesChain(parent);\n}\n/** The node a call or transparent wrapper is applied to; null for anything else. */\nfunction wrappedOf(node) {\n    if (node.type === \"CallExpression\") {\n        return node.callee;\n    }\n    return TRANSPARENT_WRAPPERS.has(node.type) ? node.expression : null;\n}\nfunction unwrapToMember(node) {\n    let current = node;\n    while (current.type !== \"MemberExpression\") {\n        current = wrappedOf(current);\n        if (!current) {\n            return null;\n        }\n    }\n    return current;\n}\nfunction measureChain(outer) {\n    let hops = 0;\n    let everyHopCalled = true;\n    let current = outer;\n    while (current) {\n        hops += 1;\n        everyHopCalled = everyHopCalled && isCalled(current);\n        const inner = unwrapToMember(current.object);\n        if (!inner) {\n            return { hops, everyHopCalled, root: rootOf(current.object) };\n        }\n        current = inner;\n    }\n    return { hops, everyHopCalled, root: null };\n}\nfunction rootOf(node) {\n    let current = node;\n    while (current.type === \"CallExpression\" ||\n        current.type === \"TSNonNullExpression\") {\n        current =\n            current.type === \"CallExpression\" ? current.callee : current.expression;\n    }\n    return current;\n}\nfunction isExemptRoot(root, allowedRoots) {\n    if (EXEMPT_ROOT_TYPES.has(root.type)) {\n        return true;\n    }\n    return root.type === \"Identifier\" && allowedRoots.has(root.name);\n}\nfunction reportData(node, hops, max, sourceCode) {\n    const text = sourceCode.getText(node);\n    const chain = text.length > CHAIN_TEXT_LIMIT\n        ? `${text.slice(0, CHAIN_TEXT_LIMIT - 3)}...`\n        : text;\n    return { chain, depth: String(hops), max: String(max) };\n}\nexport default {\n    meta: {\n        type: \"suggestion\",\n        docs: {\n            description: \"Enforce a maximum member-access chain depth (Law of Demeter); fluent all-call chains, this, and well-known globals are exempt\",\n        },\n        schema: [\n            {\n                type: \"object\",\n                properties: {\n                    max: { type: \"integer\", minimum: 1 },\n                    allowRoots: { type: \"array\", items: { type: \"string\" } },\n                },\n                additionalProperties: false,\n            },\n        ],\n        messages: {\n            chainTooDeep: \"Member chain '{{chain}}' reaches {{depth}} hops deep (max {{max}}); ask the direct collaborator for what you need\",\n        },\n    },\n    create(context) {\n        const options = context.options[0] ?? {};\n        const max = options.max ?? DEFAULT_MAX;\n        const allowedRoots = new Set([\n            ...DEFAULT_ALLOWED_ROOTS,\n            ...(options.allowRoots ?? []),\n        ]);\n        const sourceCode = context.sourceCode;\n        return {\n            MemberExpression(node) {\n                if (continuesChain(node)) {\n                    return;\n                }\n                const { hops, everyHopCalled, root } = measureChain(node);\n                if (hops <= max || everyHopCalled || isExemptRoot(root, allowedRoots)) {\n                    return;\n                }\n                context.report({\n                    node,\n                    messageId: \"chainTooDeep\",\n                    data: reportData(node, hops, max, sourceCode),\n                });\n            },\n        };\n    },\n};\n","numLines":165,"startLine":1,"totalLines":165}},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"call_dfa19a3c029e4a08b67bbd6c","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_7c1c249bae0448c9aea495e0","type":"tool_result","content":"import {readFileSync} from 'node:fs';\nimport {dirname, basename, join} from 'node:path';\nimport {fileURLToPath} from 'node:url';\nimport eslint from '@eslint/js';\nimport markdown from '@eslint/markdown';\nimport reLint from '@re-cinq/eslint-plugin-re-lint';\nimport tseslint from 'typescript-eslint';\nimport {parse as parseYaml} from 'yaml';\n\n// layers.yaml is the readable declaration of the architecture; this hands it\n// to no-cross-layer-import.\n//\n// The rule keys packages by `<package>/src/`, which suits a monorepo of\n// packages and not a single package whose code sits at ./src. Left to find\n// layers.yaml itself the rule would resolve every file as `src/...`, match no\n// package, and report nothing - adopted in appearance, enforcing nothing. So\n// the entries are re-homed under this checkout's own directory name with the\n// root moved one level up, which is the shape the matcher expects.\n//\n// Paths come from this file's own URL rather than process.cwd(), so running\n// eslint from a subdirectory cannot silently disable the rule.\n// scripts/eslint-layers.test.ts fails if this ever stops reporting.\nconst repoRoot = dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));\nconst declaredLayers = parseYaml(readFileSync(join(repoRoot, 'layers.yaml'), 'utf8')).layers.src;\n\n// Shared with eslint.config.backlog.mjs, which lints the same tree under the\n// two rules held out of the blocking gate. One list, so the two configs cannot\n// drift into disagreeing about what is even a source file.\n//\n// .claude/** is vendored agent tooling, maintained upstream rather than\n// here, so a change there must not be able to redden this repo's CI.\nexport const ignores = [\n  'node_modules/**',\n  'dist/**',\n  'coverage/**',\n  '.claude/**',\n  // Deliberately broken specs and ADRs - dead links, absent lead paragraphs,\n  // statuses no parser reads - kept as the fixtures the script tests assert\n  // against. Linting them would report the very faults they exist to reproduce.\n  'scripts/fixtures/**',\n];\n\nexport default tseslint.config(\n  {ignores},\n  {\n    // Scoped to TypeScript now that markdown is linted too: an unscoped block\n    // applies to every language, and JS rules do not survive a markdown AST.\n    files: ['**/*.ts'],\n    extends: [eslint.configs.recommended, ...tseslint.configs.recommended],\n    plugins: {'re-lint': reLint},\n    rules: {\n      // CLAUDE.md leads with five mandatory layers and \"no cross-layer\n      // shortcuts, no circular deps\". layers.yaml states that as data and this\n      // rule enforces it, so the architecture is a file someone can read rather\n      // than a habit that erodes.\n      're-lint/no-cross-layer-import': [\n        'error',\n        {root: dirname(repoRoot), layers: {[basename(repoRoot)]: declaredLayers}},\n      ],\n      '@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars': [\n        'error',\n        {\n          vars: 'all',\n          args: 'after-used',\n          argsIgnorePattern: '^_',\n          varsIgnorePattern: '^_',\n          caughtErrorsIgnorePattern: '^_',\n          ignoreRestSiblings: false,\n        },\n      ],\n      camelcase: 'error',\n      // CLAUDE.md: \"Tests live next to source: src/**/*.test.ts\". True of all\n      // ten test files today; this keeps it true.\n      're-lint/require-colocated-tests': 'error',\n      're-lint/no-commented-out-code': 'error',\n      // The provider layer must surface failures as AIError rather than\n      // swallowing them and fabricating a return value (CLAUDE.md, Adding a\n      // provider).\n      're-lint/no-catch-as-control-flow': 'error',\n      // Markdown is excluded because a doc quoting the code it documents is\n      // the intended state: README's example of createHalEngine and the\n      // interface blocks in specs/ are *supposed* to match src/. jscpd extracts\n      // fenced blocks and reports them as clones, so without this every\n      // accurate code sample is a lint error and the incentive is to let the\n      // docs drift. The same exclusion a jscpd config would carry; it lives\n      // here rather than in a .jscpd.json because the rule reads `ignore` from\n      // its own options and never from a config file.\n      're-lint/no-duplicate-code': ['error', {ignore: ['**/*.md']}],\n      're-lint/callee-below-caller': 'error',\n      're-lint/declare-near-use': 'error',\n      're-lint/default-export-matches-filename': 'error',\n      're-lint/max-boolean-operators': 'error',\n      're-lint/max-comment-lines': 'error',\n      're-lint/max-member-chain': 'error',\n      're-lint/no-closing-brace-comments': 'error',\n      're-lint/no-flag-params': 'error',\n      // INERT, kept as a placeholder. It needs type information and this config\n      // gives it none, so it reports nothing - verified with a textbook\n      // forwarding class, which it does not flag. The rule's own docs record the\n      // same finding for the same reason. It becomes a real guardrail only if\n      // this config adopts parserOptions.projectService; until then it is not\n      // one, and a clean run says nothing about forwarding classes.\n      're-lint/no-forwarding-class': 'error',\n      're-lint/no-hybrid-class': 'error',\n      're-lint/no-negative-names': 'error',\n      're-lint/no-nested-if': 'error',\n      're-lint/no-nested-loop': 'error',\n      're-lint/no-reexport-only-module': 'error',\n      're-lint/no-vague-names': 'error',\n      're-lint/prefer-early-return': 'error',\n      're-lint/prefer-polymorphism': 'error',\n      're-lint/require-fetch-timeout': 'error',\n      'no-console': 'error',\n      // Providers are loaded lazily so that selecting one never forces its SDK\n      // on consumers of the others, and the factories doing it are synchronous\n      // (`createProvider`, `createBedrockProvider`) - dynamic `import()` would\n      // make them async, which is a breaking API change. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_79ef9819f4ad44a2a579971a","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Tool Input Validation\n2\t\n3\t| Field  | Value                |\n4\t| ------ | -------------------- |\n5\t| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#37 |\n6\t| Status | In Progress          |\n7\t\n8\tEvery tool registered in `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` declares a JSON Schema `inputSchema` that is forwarded to the configured AI provider, and `ToolRegistry.execute` validates the model-supplied `input` against that schema before calling the tool's executor. When validation fails, `execute` returns a rejection `ToolResponse` describing what was wrong rather than throwing, so the orchestrator feeds the failure back to the model as a `tool_result` within the existing tool-round budget.\n9\t\n10\t## Validation at execute time\n11\t\n12\t- When `input` omits a property listed in `required`, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` whose `result` names the missing property as required and never invokes the executor ([validated by: rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L16)).\n13\t- When `input` supplies a property whose value does not match its declared JSON Schema type, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` naming the failing field path and expected type without invoking the executor, and neither `result` nor the emitted log record contains the offending property value ([validated by: rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L46)).\n14\t- When `input` satisfies `required`, declared property types and `enum`, `ToolRegistry.execute` invokes the executor once and passes the input object through unchanged — including undeclared extra properties — without injecting `additionalProperties: false`, coercing types or applying defaults.\n15\t- When `ToolRegistry.execute` is called with a tool name that has not been registered, it throws `Unknown tool: <name>` because an unregistered tool is a programming or configuration error rather than a recoverable input mistake.\n16\t\n17\t## Schema compilation and caching\n18\t\n19\t- A static `ToolDefinition` has its `inputSchema` compiled once at `register` time, so a schema that is not valid JSON Schema throws synchronously from `register` with an error message naming the offending tool ([validated by: throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L94), [validated by: throws at registration time naming the tool for an uncompilable schema](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L4)).\n20\t- A static tool's `inputSchema` is compiled at `register` time and reused on every `execute` call without re-reading or re-compiling `definition.inputSchema`.\n21\t- A function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource` resolves its definition on each `execute` call and validates against the `inputSchema` returned for that call, caching compiled validators by schema object reference (`WeakMap`) so distinct returned schemas each enforce their own rules.\n22\t\n23\t## Orchestrator tool-loop recovery\n24\t\n25\t- Because a schema rejection returns a `ToolResponse` instead of throwing, `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` sends the rejection `result` back to the provider as a `tool_result` message, allowing the model to issue a corrected tool call on the next round and complete the turn within `maxToolRounds` ([validated by: returns a schema rejection as a tool_result in the orchestrator loop so the model can correct the call on the next round](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L112)).\n26\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"63df993b-da0c-44dd-aced-eb85088a5e83","uuid":"daff559c-a9c2-4f57-a8d5-eb469221990b","timestamp":"2026-10-31T03:16:34.928Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/85c340bcbc04/workspace/target/specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md","content":"# When validation fails, `execute` returns a rejection `ToolResponse` describing what was wrong rather than throwing, so the orchestrator feeds the failure back to the model as a `tool_result` within the existing tool-round budget.\n\n## Validation at execute time\n\n- When `input` omits a property listed in `required`, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` whose `result` names the missing property as required and never invokes the executor ([validated by: rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L16)).\n- When `input` supplies a property whose value does not match its declared JSON Schema type, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` naming the failing field path and expected type without invoking the executor, and neither `result` nor the emitted log record contains the offending property value ([validated by: rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L46)).\n- When Insert eight lines above it and the anchor still resolves, still renders, and now points at something else entirely — the spec reads as cited while citing the wrong thing, and nothing about it looks wrong. `scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs` closes that: it resolves each anchor to the content it cited in a baseline ref, finds that content in the working copy, and rewrites the number. `--check` is the CI gate that refuses drift; a plain run is the fix.\n\n## What counts as an anchor\n\nAny relative path with a file extension followed by `#L<n>`, in any spec under `specs/<slug>/spec.md` plus `.specify/spec.md`. A link whose fragment is not a line number is not an anchor and is left alone, however much the file around it moves ([validated by: leaves a link whose fragment is not a line number untouched](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L506)). Test files are the common case, but nothing restricts it to them: a citation into a workflow, a config or a script is repointed the same way ([validated by: repoints docs, README and script citations alike](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L454), [root config](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L476), [workflow and manifest](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L490)).\n\nThe label is not part of the anchor. A descriptive label such as `[validated by]` is never touched ([validated by: leaves a descriptive label alone while syncing a short-form one beside it](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L420)). A short-form `[Lnn](../../src/X.test.ts#Lnn)` is different: its label carries no meaning beyond the number, so it is force-synced to whatever its own href says ([validated by: syncs labels even in a spec skipped for a differing anchor set](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L399)). Syncing happens after the rewrite, so a repointed href carries its label with it in the same run ([validated by: carries the label along when the href is repointed](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L354)).\n\n## The baseline is the point\n\nBaseline line numbers come from the base ref's copy of the **spec**, never from the working copy.\n\n- That is what makes a second run against the same baseline a no-op rather than a second translation ([validated by: is a no-op the second time, because the baseline is read from the base ref](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L76)).\n- `base-ref` defaults to `origin/main` ([validated by: defaults the base ref to origin/main](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L612)).\n\nThree cases have no baseline to reason from, and each is skipped rather than guessed:\n\n- A spec absent from the base ref is skipped whole. It is new, so no earlier line numbers exist to translate ([validated by: skips a spec absent from the base ref](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L234)).\n- A spec whose ordered list of cited paths differs from the base ref's is skipped whole. Its anchors were authored against the working tree ([validated by: skips a spec whose ordered anchor paths differ from the base ref](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L214)).\n- A single anchor whose line differs from the base spec's at the same position was deliberately retargeted by a spec edit. It is taken as authored, never rewritten, and counted under `retargeted (not checked)` ([validated by: takes a manually retargeted anchor as authored and never rewrites it](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L246)).\n\nSkipping suspends only the baseline comparison. Rotten anchors are still reported in every one of those cases ([validated by: still checks a spec that was skipped for a differing anchor set](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L326)).\n\n## Resolving a moved anchor\n\nThe content of the baseline line is looked up in the working copy of the same file.\n\n- Exactly one match is the answer ([validated by: moves each anchor to where the base ref's line content now lives](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L64)).\n- Lines are compared with quotes and whitespace dropped, so a formatter pass over a cited file is not drift: the anchor follows the line it cited, and a file reformatted in place reads as up to date ([validated by: follows a line a formatter rewrote, because quotes and spacing are not drift](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L651), [validated by: reads a file reformatted in place as up to date under --check](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L664)).\n- No match is `unresolved`: the cited line is gone, and a person has to decide what the spec meant ([validated by: reports an anchor whose baseline content is gone as unresolved, and leaves it alone](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L90)).\n- Several matches are scored against the four lines either side, and the candidate whose neighbourhood best reproduces the baseline's wins ([validated by: picks the occurrence whose surrounding lines match the baseline](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L144)).\n- If two candidates score equally the anchor is `unresolved` as ambiguous. It is never a coin flip ([validated by: refuses to guess when the context ties, and rewrites nothing](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L193)).\n- Two anchors citing identical content each resolve to their own occurrence rather than collapsing onto one, because every anchor is resolved from its own baseline line ([validated by: sends two identical assertions to their own occurrences](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L152)).\n\nThe consequence is a constraint on what to cite. A file built of repeated blocks — a workflow whose jobs share an identical setup, a table of near-identical rows — must be cited on a line unique to the step being cited, because the resolver will not choose between indistinguishable candidates ([validated by: tells apart duplicates that only differ four lines out](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L175)).\n\n## Rotten anchors\n\nIndependent of any baseline, an anchor must land somewhere real. Four ways it does not, all reported as `rotten` and all failing the run in both modes:\n\n- the cited file does not exist in the working tree ([validated by: reports a citation into a file that is not in the working tree](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L291)).\n- the line is past the end of the file ([validated by: reports an anchor past the end of the cited file](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L299)).\n- the line is blank, or holds only closing punctuation — `)`, `]`, `}`, `>`, `,`, `;` ([validated by: fails in both modes when the anchor lands on a blank line](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L263), [closing punctuation](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L279)).\n.github/workflows/ci.yml:97:      # `node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs` and committing the result.\n.github/workflows/ci.yml:99:        run: node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs --check origin/main","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"63df993b-da0c-44dd-aced-eb85088a5e83","uuid":"4048472d-633e-469c-978a-ca501980e522","timestamp":"2026-10-31T03:16:53.606Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"# HAL Engine spec anchor drift\n\n| Field  | Value |\n| ------ | ----- |\n| Issue  | n/a   |\n| Status | In Progress |\n\nA citation written `([validated by](../../src/X.test.ts#Lnn))` names a line, and a line number is the least stable thing a file has. Monday 07:00 UTC; only `build-chain` answers it.\n  schedule:\n    - cron: '0 7 * * 1'\n\n# Every job here only reads the checkout; the repo default is write.\npermissions:\n  contents: read\n\n# A newer push to the same branch supersedes an in-flight run. main is exempt:\n# every commit there should have its own recorded result.\nconcurrency:\n  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}\n  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}\n\njobs:\n  verify:\n    name: Verify\n    # The scheduled run exists for the dependency audit; re-running the suite on an unchanged\n    # tree every Monday would report nothing new.\n    if: github.event_name != 'schedule'\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1\n        with:\n          persist-credentials: false\n          # Full history, not for this job but for the spec anchor check below:\n          # it resolves cited content from\n          # origin/main, which a shallow clone cannot serve.\n          fetch-depth: 0\n\n      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0\n        with:\n          node-version: '22'\n          cache: npm","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"63df993b-da0c-44dd-aced-eb85088a5e83","uuid":"ac839f4f-7146-495a-bff4-1fdb10477da0","timestamp":"2026-10-31T03:20:13.790Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"name: CI\n\non:\n  pull_request:\n  push:\n    branches: [main]\n  # Manual runs: re-checking a branch against a moved main, or confirming a gate after\n  # changing one, without pushing an empty commit.\n  workflow_dispatch:\n  # An advisory published after a merge is invisible until someone opens a pull request, and this\n  # repository can go days without one. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_4b3b29647a4743ba9ba3b89e","type":"tool_result","content":"      # --ignore-scripts so `prepare` does not build on install: what a lifecycle script\n      # runs is out of this workflow's control, and the Build step below is where a broken\n      # compile should be reported. Type check catches it earlier still.\n      - name: Install\n        run: npm ci --ignore-scripts\n\n      # Every `npm run` step below is one link of the `verify` script in\n      # package.json, in the same order - scripts/verify-script.test.ts holds\n      # the two together - and kept as separate steps so a red run names the\n      # gate that failed rather than a single opaque command.\n      - name: Type check\n        run: npm run typecheck\n\n      # example/ is outside tsconfig.json's rootDir, so nothing checked the one\n      # file the README and the guide are written against.\n      - name: Type check the example\n        run: npm run typecheck:example\n\n      - name: Lint (--max-warnings 0)\n        run: npm run eslint\n\n      # Reports, never blocks. The one rule it runs is `warn`, so the step exits\n      # 0 on its own and carries no continue-on-error: a non-zero exit here now\n      # means the config itself broke, and that should fail. Its findings render\n      # as warning annotations rather than failures, which is what a report on a\n      # passing check should look like.\n      #\n      # require-statement-links counts spec statements with no test behind them.\n      # Most of what it reports needs a test written rather than a line changed,\n      # so the count is meant to be visible on every run and to fall over time.\n      # Its test-side mirror, require-spec-link, is satisfied and gates in the\n      # Lint step above. Never add a rule here to escape a red gate -\n      # eslint.config.backlog.mjs says what belongs.\n      - name: Spec traceability backlog (report)\n        run: npm run lint:backlog\n\n      - name: Format check\n        run: npm run prettier:check\n\n      # Runs the whole suite and fails it on the committed coverage floor in\n      # jest.config.js, so this is the test gate rather than an extra pass.\n      - name: Test (with coverage floor)\n        run: npm run test:coverage\n\n      - name: Build\n        run: npm run build\n\n      # Anchors drift silently: a cited file gaining or losing lines above the\n      # cited one leaves the link pointing at different content, and the spec\n      # still reads as cited. Resolves content at origin/main, which the\n      # fetch-depth: 0 above exists to provide. A red check is fixed by running\n      # `node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs` and committing the result.\n      - name: Spec anchor check\n        run: node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs --check origin/main\n\n      # A citation counts as coverage only in its statement's trailing\n      # parenthetical; one written mid-statement is dropped by the Lore job in silence,\n      # so the spec reads as cited while its coverage is zero. A red check is\n      # fixed by moving the link to the end of its statement, never by deleting\n      # it (AGENTS.md § Spec Test Links).\n      # Every fenced typescript block in the three documented files is generated\n      # from source; hand transcription is what produced the defects this catches.\n      - name: Documented code blocks\n        run: npm run docs:check\n\n      # Three rules that held only because somebody remembered them: a path in prose that resolves,\n      # a spike that says it is a spike, and an example region inside the EU.\n      - name: Documented paths resolve\n        run: npm run docs:check-paths\n\n      - name: Spike documents carry a status block\n        run: npm run docs:check-spikes\n\n      - name: Documented regions\n        run: npm run check:regions\n\n      # A line number is a derived pointer; the name is what the author cited. This catches a citation\n      # whose line moved under it, which no baseline comparison can see on a branch that edits the spec.\n      - name: Spec citations name their test\n        run: npm run spec:names\n\n      - name: Spec link placement\n        run: npm run check:spec-links\n\n      # Lead paragraphs and a spec's status-vs-coverage are ESLint's job; the\n      # one verdict a `files` glob cannot express - that an ADR's frontmatter\n      # status parses, without holding the ADR to the coverage tier - is this\n      # script's. `check:spec-status -- --coverage` lists unlinked statements\n      # and never gates.\n      - name: Spec status\n        run: npm run check:spec-status\n\n      # A release note and a commit subject have different readers, so this is a\n      # file the author writes rather than something derived from the log. The\n      # label is the escape hatch for a src/ change nothing installable observes.","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"63df993b-da0c-44dd-aced-eb85088a5e83","uuid":"eb3ce61b-d9f9-4c64-bc77-33df3bd26d66","timestamp":"2026-10-31T03:20:18.553Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"      # --ignore-scripts so `prepare` does not build on install: what a lifecycle script\n      # runs is out of this workflow's control, and the Build step below is where a broken\n      # compile should be reported. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_9c39d08c52154619a3f7f27b","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Adding a New Tool\n2\t\n3\tTools let the AI model fetch data or perform actions during a conversation. When the model decides it needs information (like weather data or a database lookup), it invokes a tool by name, the server executes it, and the result feeds back into the conversation.\n4\t\n5\tAdding a new tool takes two steps: define it and register it. The rest is automatic -- the orchestrator passes tools to the AI provider, and the client already knows how to render any tool entry.\n6\t\n7\t## Step 1: Create the tool file\n8\t\n9\tCreate a new file in `src/orchestration/tools/`. Each tool exports two things:\n10\t\n11\t- A **`ToolDefinition`** describing the tool's name, purpose, and input schema\n12\t- A **`ToolExecutor`** function that runs the tool and returns a JSON string\n13\t\n14\tHere is a complete example:\n15\t\n16\t<!-- doc-block: example/weather-tool.ts#weather-tool -->\n17\t```typescript\n18\timport type {ToolDefinition, ToolExecutor} from '@re-cinq/hal-engine';\n19\t\n20\texport const weatherTool: ToolDefinition = {\n21\t  name: 'get_weather',\n22\t  description:\n23\t    'Get the current weather for a location.\\n\\n' +\n24\t    'Use this tool when the user:\\n' +\n25\t    '* Asks about weather or temperature\\n' +\n26\t    '* Wants to know conditions at a specific place\\n' +\n27\t    '* Needs a forecast for planning\\n\\n' +\n28\t    'Returns temperature, conditions, humidity, and wind speed.',\n29\t  promptInstructions:\n30\t    'Use this when users ask about weather at a specific location. ' +\n31\t    'Call this for questions like \"What is the weather in Berlin?\" or \"Is it raining in Tokyo?\"',\n32\t  examplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],\n33\t  inputSchema: {\n34\t    type: 'object',\n35\t    properties: {\n36\t      location: {\n37\t        type: 'string',\n38\t        description: 'The city name or location to look up.',\n39\t      },\n40\t      units: {\n41\t        type: 'string',\n42\t        enum: ['celsius', 'fahrenheit'],\n43\t        description: 'Temperature units. Defaults to celsius.',\n44\t      },\n45\t    },\n46\t    required: ['location'],\n47\t  },\n48\t};\n49\t\n50\texport const executeWeather: ToolExecutor = async input => {\n51\t  const location = (input.location as string) || 'Unknown';\n52\t  const units = (input.units as string) || 'celsius';\n53\t\n54\t  // Replace with a real API call. `input` is untrusted: inputSchema shapes what the model sends, it does not enforce it.\n55\t  const result = {\n56\t    location,\n57\t    temperature: 18,\n58\t    units,\n59\t    conditions: 'Partly cloudy',\n60\t    humidity: 65,\n61\t    windSpeed: 12,\n62\t    windUnit: 'km/h',\n63\t  };\n64\t\n65\t  return JSON.stringify(result);\n66\t};\n67\t```\n68\t\n69\t### Writing a good tool description\n70\t\n71\tThe `description` field is what the AI model reads to decide when to use the tool. Be specific:\n72\t\n73\t- List the situations where the tool should be used (\"Use this tool when...\")\n74\t- Describe what the tool returns\n75\t- Give example queries if it helps\n76\t\n77\tThe more precise the description, the better the model's judgment about when to invoke it.\n78\t\n79\t### Adding prompt instructions\n80\t\n81\tThe optional `promptInstructions` field provides guidance that gets included in the AI's system prompt. Unlike `description` (which is part of the tool schema sent to the AI provider), `promptInstructions` appears in the system prompt text itself, giving higher-level behavioral rules about when and how to use the tool.\n82\t\n83\t<!-- doc-block: none -- one field of a ToolDefinition, quoted to discuss how to word it -->\n84\t```typescript\n85\tpromptInstructions:\n86\t  'Use this when users ask about weather at a specific location. ' +\n87\t  'Call this for questions like \"What is the weather in Berlin?\" or \"Is it raining in Tokyo?\"',\n88\t```\n89\t\n90\tThe `ToolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` method collects these from all registered tools, and the `PromptBuilder` assembles them into the system prompt automatically. If you don't provide `promptInstructions`, the tool still works -- it just won't have explicit guidance in the system prompt.\n91\t\n92\tUse `promptInstructions` for:\n93\t- Short, actionable rules about when to call the tool\n94\t- Critical behavioral constraints (e.g., \"MUST call this for every weather question\")\n95\t- Example queries that help the model match user intent\n96\t\n97\tDon't duplicate what's already in `description` -- keep `promptInstructions` focused on behavioral rules rather than describing inputs/outputs.\n98\t\n99\t### Adding example prompts\n100\t\n101\tThe optional `examplePrompts` field provides example queries that are shown to users in the chat interface as clickable suggestions. These are sent to the client in the WebSocket `connected` message and persist throughout the conversation.\n102\t\n103\t<!-- doc-block: none -- one field of a ToolDefinition, quoted to discuss how to word it -->\n104\t```typescript\n105\texamplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],\n106\t```\n107\t\n108\tThe `ToolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` method collects and flattens these from all registered tools. They are computed once at server startup and included in every new WebSocket connection's `connected` message.\n109\t\n110\tGuidelines:\n111\t- Write prompts as natural user questions, not technical descriptions\n112\t- Keep them short and specific -- they appear as pill-shaped buttons in the UI\n113\t- 1-2 prompts per tool is enough; the total across all tools should stay manageable\n114\t- Use realistic terminology relevant to your application domain\n115\t\n116\t### Defining the input schema\n117\t\n118\tThe `inputSchema` follows [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/) format. The model uses this to construct the correct input.\n119\t\n120\t- Use `required` to mark mandatory fields\n121\t- Add `description` to each property -- the model reads these\n122\t- Tool parameter names use `snake_case` (this is the convention from the AI provider API, wrap them in `/* eslint-disable camelcase */` comments)\n123\t\n124\t### Writing the executor\n125\t\n126\tA `ToolExecutor` is an async function that takes the tool input and returns either a string or a `ToolResponse`:\n127\t\n128\t<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->\n129\t```typescript\n130\ttype ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;\n131\t```\n132\t\n133\tThe optional `context` provides `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and `authHeaders` for tools that need to make authenticated API calls.\n134\t\n135\t- Return `JSON.stringify(result)` for most tools -- the result gets added to the conversation as a tool result message\n136\t- Cast input fields from `unknown` to their expected types\n137\t- Handle missing or unknown input gracefully (return a reasonable default or error message)\n138\t\n139\tFor tools that need to send messages directly to the client or suppress the AI's echo, return a `ToolResponse` object instead of a plain string. See [tool-responses.md](../specs/hal-engine-tool-responses/spec.md) for a full walkthrough.\n140\t\n141\t## Step 2: Register the tool\n142\t\n143\tOpen `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` and add two lines:\n144\t\n145\t<!-- doc-block: example/register-tool.ts#register -->\n146\t```typescript\n147\timport {weatherTool, executeWeather} from './weather-tool.js';\n148\t\n149\t// ... existing registrations ...\n150\t\n151\ttoolRegistry.register(weatherTool, executeWeather);\n152\t```\n153\t\n154\tThat is it. The `ToolRegistry` feeds all registered tool definitions to the chat orchestrator, which passes them to the AI provider. When the model invokes the tool, the registry looks up the executor by name and runs it.\n155\t\n156\t## What happens automatically\n157\t\n158\tOnce a tool is registered, the following work without any additional code:\n159\t\n160\t**On the backend:**\n161\t\n162\t- `toolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` collects example prompts from all tools and includes them in the WebSocket `connected` message\n163\t- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` to include tool guidance in the system prompt via `PromptBuilder`\n164\t- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getDefinitions()` to pass all tools to the AI provider\n165\t- When the provider returns a `tool_use` chunk, the message handler creates a `ToolEntry` and sends it via `entry_upsert`\n166\t- The orchestrator executes all pending tool calls in parallel with `Promise.all()`\n167\t- Tool results are added to the conversation, and the provider is re-queried (up to `maxToolRounds` rounds)\n168\t\n169\t**On the client:**\n170\t\n171\t- Tool entries can be rendered by the client using the `toolName` and `toolInput` fields\n172\t- `formatToolName()` strips common prefixes (`get_`, `calculate_`, `fetch_`, `find_`) and title-cases the remaining words. So `get_weather` becomes **Weather**\n173\t- `formatParamName()` converts `snake_case` parameter names to Title Case for display. So `wind_speed` becomes **Wind Speed**\n174\t- A spinner shows on the last tool entry until a subsequent entry arrives\n175\t\n176\t## File reference\n177\t\n178\t| File | What it contains |\n179\t|------|-----------------|\n180\t| `src/types/ai.ts` | `ToolDefinition` interface (includes `promptInstructions`, `examplePrompts`) |\n181\t| `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` | `ToolExecutor` type, `ToolResponse` interface, `ToolRegistry` class (includes `getPromptInstructions()`, `getExamplePrompts()`) |\n182\t| `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` | Tool registration (add your import and `register()` call here) |\n183\t| `src/infrastructure/builders/promptBuilder.ts` | `PromptBuilder` class that assembles the system prompt from tool instructions |\n184\t| `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` | Where tools are passed to the provider and executed |\n185\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"63df993b-da0c-44dd-aced-eb85088a5e83","uuid":"9b4ee844-0653-41f0-84d7-5c339f437b74","timestamp":"2026-10-31T03:21:01.731Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/85c340bcbc04/workspace/target/docs/adding-a-tool.md","content":"# Adding a New Tool\n\nTools let the AI model fetch data or perform actions during a conversation. When the model decides it needs information (like weather data or a database lookup), it invokes a tool by name, the server executes it, and the result feeds back into the conversation.\n\nAdding a new tool takes two steps: define it and register it. Each tool exports two things:\n\n- A **`ToolDefinition`** describing the tool's name, purpose, and input schema\n- A **`ToolExecutor`** function that runs the tool and returns a JSON string\n\nHere is a complete example:\n\n<!-- doc-block: example/weather-tool.ts#weather-tool -->\n```typescript\nimport type {ToolDefinition, ToolExecutor} from '@re-cinq/hal-engine';\n\nexport const weatherTool: ToolDefinition = {\n  name: 'get_weather',\n  description:\n    'Get the current weather for a location.\\n\\n' +\n    'Use this tool when the user:\\n' +\n    '* Asks about weather or temperature\\n' +\n    '* Wants to know conditions at a specific place\\n' +\n    '* Needs a forecast for planning\\n\\n' +\n    'Returns temperature, conditions, humidity, and wind speed.',\n  promptInstructions:\n    'Use this when users ask about weather at a specific location. ' +\n    'Call this for questions like \"What is the weather in Berlin?\" or \"Is it raining in Tokyo?\"',\n  examplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],\n  inputSchema: {\n    type: 'object',\n    properties: {\n      location: {\n        type: 'string',\n        description: 'The city name or location to look up.',\n      },\n      units: {\n        type: 'string',\n        enum: ['celsius', 'fahrenheit'],\n        description: 'Temperature units. Defaults to celsius.',\n      },\n    },\n    required: ['location'],\n  },\n};\n\nexport const executeWeather: ToolExecutor = async input => {\n  const location = (input.location as string) || 'Unknown';\n  const units = (input.units as string) || 'celsius';\n\n  // Replace with a real API call. `input` is untrusted: inputSchema shapes what the model sends, it does not enforce it.\n  const result = {\n    location,\n    temperature: 18,\n    units,\n    conditions: 'Partly cloudy',\n    humidity: 65,\n    windSpeed: 12,\n    windUnit: 'km/h',\n  };\n\n  return JSON.stringify(result);\n};\n```\n\n### Writing a good tool description\n\nThe `description` field is what the AI model reads to decide when to use the tool. Unlike `description` (which is part of the tool schema sent to the AI provider), `promptInstructions` appears in the system prompt text itself, giving higher-level behavioral rules about when and how to use the tool.\n\n<!-- doc-block: none -- one field of a ToolDefinition, quoted to discuss how to word it -->\n```typescript\npromptInstructions:\n  'Use this when users ask about weather at a specific location. ' +\n  'Call this for questions like \"What is the weather in Berlin?\" or \"Is it raining in Tokyo?\"',\n```\n\nThe `ToolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` method collects these from all registered tools, and the `PromptBuilder` assembles them into the system prompt automatically. If you don't provide `promptInstructions`, the tool still works -- it just won't have explicit guidance in the system prompt.\n\nUse `promptInstructions` for:\n- Short, actionable rules about when to call the tool\n- Critical behavioral constraints (e.g., \"MUST call this for every weather question\")\n- Example queries that help the model match user intent\n\nDon't duplicate what's already in `description` -- keep `promptInstructions` focused on behavioral rules rather than describing inputs/outputs.\n\n### Adding example prompts\n\nThe optional `examplePrompts` field provides example queries that are shown to users in the chat interface as clickable suggestions. These are sent to the client in the WebSocket `connected` message and persist throughout the conversation.\n\n<!-- doc-block: none -- one field of a ToolDefinition, quoted to discuss how to word it -->\n```typescript\nexamplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],\n```\n\nThe `ToolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` method collects and flattens these from all registered tools. They are computed once at server startup and included in every new WebSocket connection's `connected` message.\n\nGuidelines:\n- Write prompts as natural user questions, not technical descriptions\n- Keep them short and specific -- they appear as pill-shaped buttons in the UI\n- 1-2 prompts per tool is enough; the total across all tools should stay manageable\n- Use realistic terminology relevant to your application domain\n\n### Defining the input schema\n\nThe `inputSchema` follows [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/) format. The model uses this to construct the correct input.\n\n- Use `required` to mark mandatory fields\n- Add `description` to each property -- the model reads these\n- Tool parameter names use `snake_case` (this is the convention from the AI provider API, wrap them in `/* eslint-disable camelcase */` comments)\n\n### Writing the executor\n\nA `ToolExecutor` is an async function that takes the tool input and returns either a string or a `ToolResponse`:\n\n<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->\n```typescript\ntype ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;\n```\n\nThe optional `context` provides `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and `authHeaders` for tools that need to make authenticated API calls.\n\n- Return `JSON.stringify(result)` for most tools -- the result gets added to the conversation as a tool result message\n- Cast input fields from `unknown` to their expected types\n- Handle missing or unknown input gracefully (return a reasonable default or error message)\n\nFor tools that need to send messages directly to the client or suppress the AI's echo, return a `ToolResponse` object instead of a plain string. See [tool-responses.md](../specs/hal-engine-tool-responses/spec.md) for a full walkthrough.\n\n## Step 2: Register the tool\n\nOpen `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` and add two lines:\n\n<!-- doc-block: example/register-tool.ts#register -->\n```typescript\nimport {weatherTool, executeWeather} from './weather-tool.js';\n\n// ... existing registrations ...\n\ntoolRegistry.register(weatherTool, executeWeather);\n```\n\nThat is it. The `ToolRegistry` feeds all registered tool definitions to the chat orchestrator, which passes them to the AI provider. When the model invokes the tool, the registry looks up the executor by name and runs it.\n\n## What happens automatically\n\nOnce a tool is registered, the following work without any additional code:\n\n**On the backend:**\n\n- `toolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` collects example prompts from all tools and includes them in the WebSocket `connected` message\n- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` to include tool guidance in the system prompt via `PromptBuilder`\n- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getDefinitions()` to pass all tools to the AI provider\n- When the provider returns a `tool_use` chunk, the message handler creates a `ToolEntry` and sends it via `entry_upsert`\n- The orchestrator executes all pending tool calls in parallel with `Promise.all()`\n- Tool results are added to the conversation, and the provider is re-queried (up to `maxToolRounds` rounds)\n\n**On the client:**\n\n- Tool entries can be rendered by the client using the `toolName` and `toolInput` fields\n- `formatToolName()` strips common prefixes (`get_`, `calculate_`, `fetch_`, `find_`) and title-cases the remaining words. So `get_weather` becomes **Weather**\n- `formatParamName()` converts `snake_case` parameter names to Title Case for display. So `wind_speed` becomes **Wind Speed**\n- A spinner shows on the last tool entry until a subsequent entry arrives\n\n## File reference\n\n| File | What it contains |\n|------|-----------------|\n| `src/types/ai.ts` | `ToolDefinition` interface (includes `promptInstructions`, `examplePrompts`) |\n| `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` | `ToolExecutor` type, `ToolResponse` interface, `ToolRegistry` class (includes `getPromptInstructions()`, `getExamplePrompts()`) |\n| `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` | Tool registration (add your import and `register()` call here) |\n| `src/infrastructure/builders/promptBuilder.ts` | `PromptBuilder` class that assembles the system prompt from tool instructions |\n| `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` | Where tools are passed to the provider and executed |\n","numLines":185,"startLine":1,"totalLines":185}},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"call_9c39d08c52154619a3f7f27b","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_61a407cca20944f9a0508a48","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# HAL Engine\n2\t\n3\tA generic AI chat server framework with pluggable providers, tools, and transport.\n4\t\n5\tHAL Engine extracts the core patterns of building an AI-powered chat backend into a reusable library. It handles streaming responses, tool execution loops, WebSocket connections, and session management -- you bring your own AI provider, auth, and domain tools.\n6\t\n7\t## Features\n8\t\n9\t- **Multi-provider support**: AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI implemented, OpenAI and Anthropic stubbed, plus a built-in Mock. Scored per method in [Providers](#providers) — a provider can implement one of `AIProvider`'s two methods without the other\n10\t- **Tool system**: Register custom tools with a JSON Schema `inputSchema`, executed in parallel within a configurable tool loop. The schema is forwarded to the model to shape the call it produces; it is **not** enforced before your executor runs, so validate the input you are handed\n11\t- **Streaming**: Real-time WebSocket streaming with thinking tag parsing and entry-based protocol\n12\t- **Pluggable auth**: Bring your own WebSocket and HTTP authentication\n13\t- **Pluggable session store**: In-memory default, swap in Redis/database/etc.\n14\t- **Configurable prompts**: Identity, domain context, response guidelines -- all injectable\n15\t- **Express + WebSocket**: Full HTTP API and WebSocket server out of the box\n16\t\n17\t## Install\n18\t\n19\t```bash\n20\tnpm install @re-cinq/hal-engine\n21\t```\n22\t\n23\tThat is the supported install path, and the one this project releases against: every published version is built by a workflow run in this repository's CI and carries an npm provenance attestation. `npm audit signatures` verifies it, which tells you the tarball was built by a workflow of this repository from the commit the attestation names, rather than uploaded by whoever held a token. `0.2.0` was published once with a token, because the registry cannot hold a trusted publisher for a name that has never been published; every version after it is published by the release workflow from a published GitHub release, with no credential stored anywhere, and reaches you only after a maintainer approves it.\n24\t\n25\tA git specifier also resolves, and four things differ. It builds `dist/` from a checkout through the `prepare` script rather than installing a built artefact, so your install runs this package's TypeScript compiler. It carries no provenance, because provenance is produced at publish time. It pins whatever commit your lockfile recorded, not a version, so `npm outdated` has nothing to compare and a fix reaches you only when you repoint it. And npm installs a dependency under its **key**, not the package's `name`.\n26\t\n27\tThat last one has a trap in it. An existing `\"hal-engine\": \"github:…\"` entry keeps resolving after the rename — the directory is still `node_modules/hal-engine`, so `import 'hal-engine'` keeps working while the package inside it declares `@re-cinq/hal-engine`. The rename produces no error, no warning and no failed build. Worse, following the rename and switching your imports to `@re-cinq/hal-engine` is what breaks: that specifier resolves to nothing until the key is renamed too. Move to the registry specifier, or rename the key and the imports together.\n28\t\n29\t## Quick Start\n30\t\n31\t<!-- doc-block: example/server.ts#quick-start -->\n32\t```typescript\n33\timport {createHalEngine, log, ToolRegistry} from '@re-cinq/hal-engine';\n34\t\n35\tconst tools = new ToolRegistry();\n36\t\n37\ttools.register(\n38\t  {\n39\t    name: 'get_weather',\n40\t    description: 'Get current weather for a city',\n41\t    inputSchema: {\n42\t      type: 'object',\n43\t      properties: {\n44\t        city: {type: 'string', description: 'City name'},\n45\t      },\n46\t      required: ['city'],\n47\t    },\n48\t    promptInstructions: 'Use this tool when the user asks about weather in a specific city.',\n49\t    examplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],\n50\t  },\n51\t  async input => {\n52\t    const city = input.city as string;\n53\t    return `Weather in ${city}: 22C, partly cloudy, wind 12 km/h NW`;\n54\t  }\n55\t);\n56\t\n57\tconst engine = createHalEngine({\n58\t  provider: {type: 'mock'},\n59\t  prompt: {\n60\t    identity: 'You are a helpful AI assistant.',\n61\t    responseGuidelines: 'Be concise and informative.',\n62\t  },\n63\t  tools,\n64\t  auth: {\n65\t    // No `http` middleware here, so the chat routes under /api/chats answer 401 rather than serving anyone.\n66\t    ws: async req => {\n67\t      const token = req.headers.authorization;\n68\t      if (!token) return null;\n69\t      return {id: 'user-1'};\n70\t    },"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"63df993b-da0c-44dd-aced-eb85088a5e83","uuid":"4a34f4da-4e19-439c-b3ac-2aa491cfbc02","timestamp":"2026-10-31T03:21:42.528Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/85c340bcbc04/workspace/target/README.md","content":"# HAL Engine\n\nA generic AI chat server framework with pluggable providers, tools, and transport.\n\nHAL Engine extracts the core patterns of building an AI-powered chat backend into a reusable library. It handles streaming responses, tool execution loops, WebSocket connections, and session management -- you bring your own AI provider, auth, and domain tools.\n\n## Features\n\n- **Multi-provider support**: AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI implemented, OpenAI and Anthropic stubbed, plus a built-in Mock. Scored per method in [Providers](#providers) — a provider can implement one of `AIProvider`'s two methods without the other\n- **Tool system**: Register custom tools with a JSON Schema `inputSchema`, executed in parallel within a configurable tool loop. The schema is forwarded to the model to shape the call it produces; it is **not** enforced before your executor runs, so validate the input you are handed\n- **Streaming**: Real-time WebSocket streaming with thinking tag parsing and entry-based protocol\n- **Pluggable auth**: Bring your own WebSocket and HTTP authentication\n- **Pluggable session store**: In-memory default, swap in Redis/database/etc.\n- **Configurable prompts**: Identity, domain context, response guidelines -- all injectable\n- **Express + WebSocket**: Full HTTP API and WebSocket server out of the box\n\n## Install\n\n```bash\nnpm install @re-cinq/hal-engine\n```\n\nThat is the supported install path, and the one this project releases against: every published version is built by a workflow run in this repository's CI and carries an npm provenance attestation. `npm audit signatures` verifies it, which tells you the tarball was built by a workflow of this repository from the commit the attestation names, rather than uploaded by whoever held a token. `0.2.0` was published once with a token, because the registry cannot hold a trusted publisher for a name that has never been published; every version after it is published by the release workflow from a published GitHub release, with no credential stored anywhere, and reaches you only after a maintainer approves it.\n\nA git specifier also resolves, and four things differ. It builds `dist/` from a checkout through the `prepare` script rather than installing a built artefact, so your install runs this package's TypeScript compiler. It carries no provenance, because provenance is produced at publish time. It pins whatever commit your lockfile recorded, not a version, so `npm outdated` has nothing to compare and a fix reaches you only when you repoint it. And npm installs a dependency under its **key**, not the package's `name`.\n\nThat last one has a trap in it. An existing `\"hal-engine\": \"github:…\"` entry keeps resolving after the rename — the directory is still `node_modules/hal-engine`, so `import 'hal-engine'` keeps working while the package inside it declares `@re-cinq/hal-engine`. The rename produces no error, no warning and no failed build. Worse, following the rename and switching your imports to `@re-cinq/hal-engine` is what breaks: that specifier resolves to nothing until the key is renamed too. Move to the registry specifier, or rename the key and the imports together.\n\n## Quick Start\n\n<!-- doc-block: example/server.ts#quick-start -->\n```typescript\nimport {createHalEngine, log, ToolRegistry} from '@re-cinq/hal-engine';\n\nconst tools = new ToolRegistry();\n\ntools.register(\n  {\n    name: 'get_weather',\n    description: 'Get current weather for a city',\n    inputSchema: {\n      type: 'object',\n      properties: {\n        city: {type: 'string', description: 'City name'},\n      },\n      required: ['city'],\n    },\n    promptInstructions: 'Use this tool when the user asks about weather in a specific city.',\n    examplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],\n  },\n  async input => {\n    const city = input.city as string;\n    return `Weather in ${city}: 22C, partly cloudy, wind 12 km/h NW`;\n  }\n);\n\nconst engine = createHalEngine({\n  provider: {type: 'mock'},\n  prompt: {\n    identity: 'You are a helpful AI assistant.',\n    responseGuidelines: 'Be concise and informative.',\n  },\n  tools,\n  auth: {\n    // No `http` middleware here, so the chat routes under /api/chats answer 401 rather than serving anyone.\n    ws: async req => {\n      const token = req.headers.authorization;\n      if (!token) return null;\n      return {id: 'user-1'};\n    },","numLines":70,"startLine":1,"totalLines":208}},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"call_61a407cca20944f9a0508a48","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_2822e8c6866046eba91546e3","type":"tool_result","content":"1:# HAL Engine System Specification\n3:## Overview\n5:HAL Engine is a generic, production-ready AI chat server framework designed to abstract away the complexity of building AI-powered chat backends. It provides a pluggable architecture for AI providers, tools, authentication, session management, and transport, allowing developers to focus on domain-specific logic rather than infrastructure plumbing.\n7:The system handles core patterns including streaming responses, tool execution loops, WebSocket connections, session persistence, and message orchestration. It is structured as a layered application with clear separation of concerns from core types through infrastructure and transport.\n14:## Key Capabilities\n16:### 1. Multi-Provider Support\n26:### 2. Tool System\n28:- Dynamic tool registration via `ToolRegistry`\n29:- JSON Schema tool definitions, declared per tool and forwarded to the model; the schema describes the input the model should produce and is NOT enforced before the executor runs\n30:- Parallel tool execution within configurable tool loops\n32:- Context-aware tool execution: the executor receives the caller's identity (`userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`) and the auth headers the session carries, forwarded from the WebSocket upgrade or the HTTP chat request, not the conversation history\n33:- Configurable maximum tool loop iterations (default: 5)\n35:### 3. Real-Time Streaming\n43:### 4. Pluggable Authentication\n50:### 5. Session Management\n58:### 6. Configurable Prompts\n64:### 7. HTTP + WebSocket Server\n73:## Core Data Model\n75:### Message Flow\n88:- `EntrySkipMessage`: Skip tool/response generation\n93:### Session Model\n106:- `AssistantEntry`: AI-generated response with tool calls\n111:### AI Communication Model\n118:- `ToolCallContent`: Structured tool call representation\n119:- `ToolResultContent`: Structured tool result representation\n140:## User Roles\n142:### 1. **System Administrator**\n147:- Sets rate limits and tool execution constraints\n151:### 2. **Application Developer**\n154:- Registers domain-specific tools via `ToolRegistry`\n160:### 3. **End User**\n165:- Observes tool execution through entry protocol\n168:### 4. **AI Model (Provider)**\n171:- Generates text responses and tool calls\n174:- Validates tool calls against schemas\n178:## Business Rules\n180:### 1. Tool Execution\n183:- Maximum tool loop iterations enforce termination (prevents infinite loops)\n188:### 2. Message Ordering\n191:- Tool results must follow corresponding tool calls\n322 .specify/spec.md","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"63df993b-da0c-44dd-aced-eb85088a5e83","uuid":"b7f9e601-a2aa-4432-8454-9361872e3798","timestamp":"2026-10-31T03:22:05.841Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"1:# HAL Engine System Specification\n3:## Overview\n5:HAL Engine is a generic, production-ready AI chat server framework designed to abstract away the complexity of building AI-powered chat backends. It provides a pluggable architecture for AI providers, tools, authentication, session management, and transport, allowing developers to focus on domain-specific logic rather than infrastructure plumbing.\n7:The system handles core patterns including streaming responses, tool execution loops, WebSocket connections, session persistence, and message orchestration. It is structured as a layered application with clear separation of concerns from core types through infrastructure and transport.\n14:## Key Capabilities\n16:### 1. Multi-Provider Support\n26:### 2. Tool System\n28:- Dynamic tool registration via `ToolRegistry`\n29:- JSON Schema tool definitions, declared per tool and forwarded to the model; the schema describes the input the model should produce and is NOT enforced before the executor runs\n30:- Parallel tool execution within configurable tool loops\n32:- Context-aware tool execution: the executor receives the caller's identity (`userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`) and the auth headers the session carries, forwarded from the WebSocket upgrade or the HTTP chat request, not the conversation history\n33:- Configurable maximum tool loop iterations (default: 5)\n35:### 3. Real-Time Streaming\n43:### 4. Pluggable Authentication\n50:### 5. Session Management\n58:### 6. Configurable Prompts\n64:### 7. HTTP + WebSocket Server\n73:## Core Data Model\n75:### Message Flow\n88:- `EntrySkipMessage`: Skip tool/response generation\n93:### Session Model\n106:- `AssistantEntry`: AI-generated response with tool calls\n111:### AI Communication Model\n118:- `ToolCallContent`: Structured tool call representation\n119:- `ToolResultContent`: Structured tool result representation\n140:## User Roles\n142:### 1. **System Administrator**\n147:- Sets rate limits and tool execution constraints\n151:### 2. **Application Developer**\n154:- Registers domain-specific tools via `ToolRegistry`\n160:### 3. **End User**\n165:- Observes tool execution through entry protocol\n168:### 4. **AI Model (Provider)**\n171:- Generates text responses and tool calls\n174:- Validates tool calls against schemas\n178:## Business Rules\n180:### 1. Tool Execution\n183:- Maximum tool loop iterations enforce termination (prevents infinite loops)\n188:### 2. Message Ordering\n191:- Tool results must follow corresponding tool calls\n322 .specify/spec.md","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"call_2822e8c6866046eba91546e3","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

{result: response} : response;\n}\n\nexport type ToolDefinitionSource = ToolDefinition | (() => ToolDefinition);\n\nexport interface RegisteredTool {\n  definition: ToolDefinition;\n  execute: ToolExecutor;\n}\n\ntype ValidatorFor = (definition: ToolDefinition) => ValidateFunction;\n\ninterface StoredTool {\n  definitionSource: ToolDefinitionSource;\n  execute: ToolExecutor;\n  validatorFor: ValidatorFor;\n}\n\nexport class ToolRegistry {\n  private readonly tools = new Map<string, StoredTool>();\n\n  private resolveDefinition(source: ToolDefinitionSource): ToolDefinition {\n    return typeof source === 'function' ? source() : source;\n  }\n\n  register(definitionSource: ToolDefinitionSource, execute: ToolExecutor): void {\n    const resolved = this.resolveDefinition(definitionSource);\n    const validatorFor: ValidatorFor =\n      typeof definitionSource === 'function'\n        ? definition => schemaValidator(resolved.name, definition.inputSchema)\n        : staticValidator(resolved.name, resolved.inputSchema);\n    this.tools.set(resolved.name, {definitionSource, execute, validatorFor});\n  }\n\n  get(name: string): RegisteredTool | undefined {\n    const tool = this.tools.get(name);\n    if (!tool) return undefined;\n    return {definition: this.resolveDefinition(tool.definitionSource), execute: tool.execute};\n  }\n\n  getDefinitions(): ToolDefinition[] {\n    return [...this.tools.values()].map(t => this.resolveDefinition(t.definitionSource));\n  }\n\n  getPromptInstructions(): string[] {\n    return this.getDefinitions()\n      .filter(t => t.promptInstructions)\n      .map(t => `${t.name}: ${t.promptInstructions}`);\n  }\n\n  getExamplePrompts(): string[] {\n    return this.getDefinitions().flatMap(t => t.examplePrompts ?? []);\n  }\n\n  has(name: string): boolean {\n    return this.tools.has(name);\n  }\n\n  /**\n   * Validates `input` against the resolved `inputSchema` and returns the rejection as a `ToolResponse` without running the executor; the only throw is `Unknown tool: <name>` — full contract in specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md.\n   */\n  async execute(name: string, input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext): Promise<ToolResponse> {\n    const tool = this.tools.get(name);\n    if (!tool) {\n      log.warn('tool', 'tool not found', {name});\n      throw new Error(`Unknown tool: ${name}`);\n    }\n    const validator = tool.validatorFor(this.resolveDefinition(tool.definitionSource));\n    if (!validator(input)) {\n      const rejections = describeSchemaErrors(validator.errors ?? []);\n      log.warn('tool', 'input rejected by inputSchema', {name, rejections});\n      return {result: `Tool input rejected: ${rejections.join('; ')}`};\n    }\n    log.info('tool', 'executing', {name, inputKeys: Object.keys(input)});\n    const rawResult = await tool.execute(input, context);\n    const response = normalizeToolResponse(rawResult);\n    log.info('tool', 'execution complete', {\n      name,\n      rawType: typeof rawResult,\n      clientMessageCount: response.clientMessages?.length ?? 0,\n      clientMessageTypes: response.clientMessages?.map(m => m.type) ?? {result: response} : response;\n}\n\nexport type ToolDefinitionSource = ToolDefinition | (() => ToolDefinition);\n\nexport interface RegisteredTool {\n  definition: ToolDefinition;\n  execute: ToolExecutor;\n}\n\ninterface StoredTool {\n  definitionSource: ToolDefinitionSource;\n  execute: ToolExecutor;\n  validateInput: ValidateFunction;\n}\n\nexport class ToolRegistry {\n  private readonly tools = new Map<string, StoredTool>();\n\n  private resolveDefinition(source: ToolDefinitionSource): ToolDefinition {\n    return typeof source === 'function' ? source() : source;\n  }\n\n  register(definition: ToolDefinitionSource, execute: ToolExecutor): void {\n    const resolved = this.resolveDefinition(definition);\n    const validateInput = compileSchema(resolved.name, resolved.inputSchema);\n    this.tools.set(resolved.name, {definitionSource: definition, execute, validateInput});\n  }\n\n  get(name: string): RegisteredTool | undefined {\n    const tool = this.tools.get(name);\n    if (!tool) return undefined;\n    return {definition: this.resolveDefinition(tool.definitionSource), execute: tool.execute};\n  }\n\n  getDefinitions(): ToolDefinition[] {\n    return [...this.tools.values()].map(t => this.resolveDefinition(t.definitionSource));\n  }\n\n  getPromptInstructions(): string[] {\n    return this.getDefinitions()\n      .filter(t => t.promptInstructions)\n      .map(t => `${t.name}: ${t.promptInstructions}`);\n  }\n\n  getExamplePrompts(): string[] {\n    return this.getDefinitions().flatMap(t => t.examplePrompts ?? []);\n  }\n\n  has(name: string): boolean {\n    return this.tools.has(name);\n  }\n\n  async execute(name: string, input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext): Promise<ToolResponse> {\n    const tool = this.tools.get(name);\n    if (!tool) {\n      log.warn('tool', 'tool not found', {name});\n      throw new Error(`Unknown tool: ${name}`);\n    }\n    log.info('tool', 'executing', {name, inputKeys: Object.keys(input)});\n    const rawResult = await tool.execute(input, context);\n    const response = normalizeToolResponse(rawResult);\n    log.info('tool', 'execution complete', {\n      name,\n      rawType: typeof rawResult,\n      clientMessageCount: response.clientMessages?.length ?? 0,\n      clientMessageTypes: response.clientMessages?.map(m => m.type) ?? [],\n      suppressAssistantResponse: response.suppressAssistantResponse ?? false,\n    });\n    return response;\n  }\n}\n\nconst ajv = new Ajv({strict: false, validateFormats: false, allErrors: true});\n\nfunction compileSchema(toolName: string, schema: Record<string, unknown>): ValidateFunction {\n  try {\n    return ajv.compile(schema);\n  } catch (error) {\n    throw new Error(`Invalid inputSchema for tool \"${toolName}\": ${(error as Error).message}`);\n  }\n}\n","userModified":false},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"call_09f686cf0b554831ac013e70","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

   {\n        name: 'get_reading',\n        description: 'Read a sensor',\n        inputSchema: {\n          type: 'object',\n          properties: {sensorId: {type: 'string'}},\n          required: ['sensorId'],\n        },\n      },\n      async input => {\n        executorInputs.push(input);\n        return 'reading recorded';\n      }\n    );\n\n    await registry.execute('get_reading', async () => 'reading recorded'\n    );\n\n    for (let round = 0; round < 10; round++) await registry.execute('get_reading', {sensorId: 'temp-1'});\n\n    expect(compileSpy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);\n    compileSpy.mockRestore();\n  });\n\n  it('validates a function-valued definition against the schema returned for that call, not a stale cached one', resolution = 0;\n    registry.register(\n      () => {\n        const schema = schemas[resolution];\n        resolution += 1;\n        return {\n          name: 'get_forecast',\n          description: 'Get forecast for a region',\n          inputSchema: schema,\n        };\n      },\n      async () => 'unreachable'\n    );\n\n    const first = await registry.execute('get_forecast', {});\n    const second = await registry.execute('get_forecast', {});\n\n    expect({first: first.result, second: second.result}).toEqual({\n      first: expect.stringContaining('location'),\n      second: });\n});\n"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":0},"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"63df993b-da0c-44dd-aced-eb85088a5e83","uuid":"254e3d13-c194-472a-bc1c-2089ffd7098c","timestamp":"2026-10-31T03:26:11.909Z"}
